title: TSFAdv: Frequency-Guided Black-Box Adversarial Attacks on Time Series Forecasting
one_liner: Adversarial attacks on time-series forecasts can trick models by perturbing the frequency content of the input signal, even with limited query access.
lead: Time-series forecasting models predict future values in streams like electricity demand or sensor readings. These models, when deployed as black-box services (where you only see predictions, not internals), are vulnerable to carefully crafted fake inputs called adversarial perturbations. This paper shows that an attacker can make high-quality forecasting models fail dramatically by tweaking the frequency content of the input signal in a smart way, even when restricted to only 200 queries.

problem.h2: Why time-series forecasting is fragile to frequency manipulation
paras: Time-series forecasting models learn patterns from sequences of numbers over time. When deployed as a black-box API (you send in past values, get back a forecast, but cannot inspect the internals), these models are usually trusted to work correctly. A beginner might assume that random noise or small tweaks to the input would barely affect the output.

But the paper reveals a deeper vulnerability: these models are extremely sensitive to changes in the frequency content of the signal. If you carefully modify which frequencies are present (the pitch and speed of oscillations in the data), the model's predictions break even though the overall "shape" of the data looks similar to a human eye. An attacker with just 200 allowed queries can find exactly which frequency changes cause the biggest forecasting errors.

callout.html: Tweaking the frequency spectrum of time-series input can fool the best forecasting models, even with a tiny budget of allowed queries.

panels.title: 1. Normal forecast
panels.caption: Time-series model receives clean past data and predicts future values accurately.

panels.title: 2. Attacker probes frequencies
panels.caption: With each query, the attacker learns which frequency bands the model relies on most.

panels.title: 3. Crafted perturbation in frequency domain
panels.viz_args: Flip phase / boost amplitude at vulnerable frequencies
panels.caption: The attacker constructs a targeted frequency-domain change that maximizes forecast error.

panels.title: 4. Modified input sent to model
panels.caption: The frequency-perturbed signal looks deceptively similar to humans but breaks the model.

panels.title: 5. Forecast collapses
panels.caption: The model outputs predictions far from the true future values; trajectory shape is totally wrong.

steps.text: Attacker sends signals with different frequency components, observing how each changes the forecast error.
A random-search method estimates which direction in frequency space causes the most damage, without needing the model's internal weights.
Based on sensitivity estimates, construct a targeted change to magnitude and phase of specific frequencies.
Instead of checking single-point error, measure whether the entire predicted sequence has wrong shape and direction.
Repeat probing and refinement until 200 queries are exhausted, reaching maximum forecast degradation.

paras: The paper targets the frequency spectrum of the input signal: specifically, the amplitude and phase at different frequencies. By carefully perturbing these, without access to the model's weights or training process, an attacker can degrade forecasts dramatically.

hidden.name: frequency sensitivity score
paras: The paper measures a quantity that does not appear in standard model outputs: which frequencies the model depends on most for accurate predictions. A time-series signal can be decomposed into a sum of sine waves at different frequencies (this is called the Fourier transform). Some frequencies might be critical for the model's logic, while others are noise.

The paper estimates this sensitivity by testing: if I boost or flip the phase of frequency F, how much worse do predictions become? Frequencies with big effects on error are sensitive; frequencies with no effect are not. The attacker uses these sensitivity scores to know where to strike.

heat.caption: Darker means more sensitive to perturbation. Model relies on some frequencies heavily, barely on others.

reads.html: Think of a song made from many instruments (frequencies). A singer depends on the melody (one key frequency) but not on every background note. If you remove the melody, the singer loses their way; if you remove random noise, they do not notice.

The paper embeds frequency-domain priors into Natural Evolution Strategies (a random-search optimization method). This estimates which way to nudge frequency perturbations to maximize forecast error, ranking which frequencies matter most.

paras: Time-series forecasting models are trained on real data with natural frequencies (seasonal patterns like daily/weekly cycles, trends, noise). When the model learns to forecast, it implicitly learns which frequencies signal true future patterns and which are random wiggles to ignore.

If an attacker removes or inverts the frequencies the model trusts most, the model has no reliable signal left. For example, if the model learned that a strong daily cycle means steady demand tomorrow, but the attacker removes the daily cycle from today's signal, the model cannot forecast accurately. The frequencies the model learned are the frequencies it needs. Change those, and prediction breaks.

The attacker can find these critical frequencies quickly using a random-search method (Natural Evolution Strategies) that estimates sensitivity without needing the model's internal workings. Instead of guessing blindly, this method tries small random perturbations around a current best guess and keeps the direction that causes more error. By repeating this process, it narrows in on the most damaging frequency changes. After 200 queries, the attacker has a frequency-domain adversarial input that maximizes error.

stages.s: Time series with natural frequencies (daily, weekly, noise)
Model learned: trust these frequencies, ignore those
Attacker perturbs trusted frequencies using evolution strategies
Signal now has wrong frequencies; model has no reliable pattern
Forecast is wrong; trajectory has wrong shape and direction

math.words: forecast_error equals a distance metric between predicted and true trajectory. Attacker aims to maximize this by adding frequency perturbation delta_f to the input spectrum.
math.equation: max_delta_f [ DTW(forecast(input + delta_f), true_future) + lambda * SME(forecast(input + delta_f), true_future) ]
symbols: the frequency-domain perturbation (amplitude and phase changes at each frequency)
Dynamic Time Warping: a distance metric that measures how different two sequences' shapes are
Slope Misalignment Error: measures whether the directions and speeds of change are wrong
weight balancing the two error metrics
original time series plus the adversarial frequency perturbation

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scenario: 4-step forecast of electricity demand, true values [95, 100, 102, 105] kWh.
Model predicts [96, 99, 101, 106] without attack: DTW distance ≈ 2.0, SME ≈ 0.1, total error ≈ 0.1+0.1=0.2.
Attacker removes the weekly frequency (critical for demand patterns) from input: model now predicts [80, 85, 88, 92].
New DTW distance ≈ 20.0, SME ≈ 5.0, total error ≈ 20.0+5.0=25.0.
Error jumped 125x. One carefully chosen frequency removal broke the forecast.

math.note: The attacker searches over frequency perturbations delta_f to maximize this error, using random search (evolution strategies) within 200 queries.

bars.h2: Forecast quality before and after attack

charts.title: Robust baseline (no attack)
charts.note: Model forecasts well on clean input; operators trust its predictions.

charts.title: After frequency-domain adversarial attack
charts.note: Same model with adversarial frequency perturbations: accuracy drops 38% (DTW), shape degrades 26% (SME). Existing defenses fail.

items.html: The attacker has only 200 queries. If the frequency space is very high-dimensional, 200 random samples may not find the best attack direction. With more queries allowed, evolution strategies would narrow in more precisely on worse perturbations, because each extra sample steers closer to the worst error.

If a deployment smooths or filters the input before feeding it to the model, high-frequency perturbations may be removed. The attack targets frequencies the model sees, not frequencies the attacker can inject.
The paper shows existing defenses (adversarial training, input perturbation) do not work. But a model trained explicitly to resist frequency perturbations might work.

items.b: Attack succeeds when model relies on few, vulnerable frequencies.
items.html: If a forecasting model learns many overlapping frequency cues (so losing one does not break everything), removing one frequency hurts less. The attack is most dangerous when the model uses only a few critical frequencies.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple LSTM or RNN time-series forecasting model trained on synthetic data with a strong daily cycle (e.g., sine wave plus noise). Then implement TSFAdv: use random search (evolution strategies) to find a frequency perturbation that maximizes forecast error under 200 queries. Measure error before and after using DTW and SME metrics.
demo.closing: The demo must show that a frequency perturbation found in just 200 queries can degrade forecast error by 30%+ on an undefended model, even though the adversarial input looks visually similar to the clean data.
